title: A House That Remembers Every Tenant
hook: A rooming house slated for demolition begins rearranging itself into bedrooms from every decade of its existence.
truth: The house is a memory engine built from grief, rent receipts, and a landlord's old bargain with something beneath the foundation.

monster.name: The Tenant Archive
monster.instinct: To preserve every tenant forever by making them part of the house.
weaknesses: opening the sealed root cellar at sunrise

countdown.label: First Sign
countdown.text: A tenant wakes in a room decorated for 1978, with snow outside the window in June.

countdown.label: First Loss
countdown.text: A new renter disappears and their name appears on an old mailbox.

countdown.label: Expansion
countdown.text: The house gains an extra hallway visible only to people carrying unpaid bills.

countdown.label: Pressure
countdown.text: Personal objects vanish across the block and reappear in rooms no one can enter.

countdown.label: Crisis
countdown.text: The demolition crew opens a wall and hears dozens of people breathing inside.

countdown.label: Finale
countdown.text: The house folds the whole street into one impossible interior and begins assigning rooms.

clues.text: A rent ledger contains names that do not appear in any city record.
The plaster hides a neat grid of watches, photographs, keys, and baby teeth.
The cellar door unlocks only when the sun hits the kitchen window.
Suite 2B appears in tax records but not on any floor plan.
A receipt written as an apology is hidden inside the baseboard.
A lullaby moves from room to room in the order tenants disappeared.

keeperHints: Treat rooms as emotional evidence, not puzzle boxes only.
Let the house preserve people with terrible tenderness.
Use practical tenant details: mail, rent, repairs, bad locks, old carpet.
revealPolicy: Reveal the house's motive through tenant rooms and stolen keepsakes before exposing the bargain.
automationSafety: Do not trap a player character permanently without a clear escape path.
Keep memory alteration reversible unless the user explicitly wants harsher stakes.
